# Results — Study 366 (Merger-Arbitrage)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The classic **merger-arb
coupon**: after an all-cash takeover is announced, the target trades a few percent below
the offer — buy it, hold to close, pocket the spread. We harvest realized arb returns from
a hardcoded book of **20 real announced all-cash US M&A deals** (a deliberate mix of clean
closes and high-profile breaks), and ask whether the average deal pays **more** than fair
compensation for the deal-break tail. Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Deal book | **20** real announced **all-cash** US M&A deals, 2020–2024 (offer, announce/close-or-break dates, outcome, documented entry & pre-deal closes) |
| Window | announces 2020-10-21 → resolutions through 2024-12-31 (**as-of 2026-06-22**) |
| Entry | target close ~1 trading day **after** the announcement (no look-ahead — you buy after the deal is public) |
| Break mark | target snaps back to its ~1-week-**pre**-deal standalone close |
| Price confirmation | yfinance daily adjusted closes for still-listed targets (FHN, SIMO) confirm the documented marks; acquired targets are delisted and unavailable, so the documented closes are the reproducible datum |
| Costs | one-way bps charged on entry **and** exit of each deal (one round-trip per deal); long-only on the target — no borrow |

> **Data caveat (named on the Signal axis).** Acquired targets are **delisted** and vanish
> from yfinance, so the entry/pre-deal closes are **documented public closes** carried in the
> deal table, confirmed against live data only for the two surviving (broken-deal) names. The
> book is also **small (20 deals) and curated**, with a deliberately *high* break share
> (**4 / 20 = 20%**, vs a historical base rate nearer 5–10%) so the break tail is visible in a
> small sample — this makes the realized mean a *conservative, illustrative* read, not a
> precise alpha estimate. The verdict does **not** hinge on the exact break count: it hinges
> on the fact that a few breaks of −20% to −40% each dominate the mean of a spread book, so
> the average deal's edge is statistically indistinguishable from zero on any honest sample.

## The signal — realized arb return per deal vs the spread you "see"

You enter at a gross spread; you realize the spread **only if the deal closes**, and a
deep loss if it breaks. The believers quote the first column; the tape pays the last.

| measure | value |
|---|--:|
| gross spread at entry (all 20 deals) | **+8.99%** |
| spread on the 16 deals that **closed** | **+7.09%** |
| mean realized return on the 4 **breaks** | **−19.39%** |
| **mean realized arb return (all 20 deals)** | **+1.79%** |
| median realized arb return | +3.83% |
| win-rate (deals that closed/paid) | **80%** |
| return skew | **−0.91** (fat left tail) |

The pitch number — *"a 7–9% spread, market-neutral, just wait for the close"* — is **gross
of the break tail**. Count the four breaks honestly (JetBlue/Spirit blocked, TD/First
Horizon terminated, Avangrid/PNM collapsed, MaxLinear/Silicon Motion terminated) and the
average deal returns **+1.79%**, because four ~−19% losers eat most of what sixteen ~+7%
winners earn. An 80% win-rate with a deep, rare loser is **exactly** the shape of selling
insurance.

## Is +1.79% real? — the small-sample, fat-tail test

| test | value | reading |
|---|--:|---|
| one-sample Welch *t* (per-deal mean vs 0) | **+0.67** | **fails t ≥ 2** |
| bootstrap *p*(mean ≤ 0), 20,000 draws | **0.24** | ~1 in 4 resamples is ≤ 0 |
| bootstrap 90% CI of the mean | **[−2.65%, +5.90%]** | straddles zero |

The per-deal mean is **positive but not significant**: a 90% bootstrap CI that runs from
**−2.6% to +5.9%** cannot rule out zero, and a quarter of resamples come out non-positive.
With only 20 deals and a return distribution dominated by its left tail, the spread book is
**statistically indistinguishable from a fair bet** — you are paid a premium that, on this
sample, roughly equals the insurance you are writing.

> **A note on the annualized number.** Annualizing each deal's return by its (short) holding
> period gives a mean of **+5.66%/yr** and a *t* of **2.09** — but that figure is **not** a
> Signal-axis statistic: annualizing a handful of overlapping few-month bets inflates *t* by
> treating each deal as if it scaled to a full year independently. The honest, per-bet test
> is the one above (*t* = 0.67). We report the annualized number only to show where the
> "merger-arb makes ~mid-single-digits a year" lore comes from — and that it does not survive
> an honest standard error.

## Costs barely move it — frequency and the tail are the story

| one-way cost | gross mean | net mean | net *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps  | +1.79% | +1.69% | 0.63 |
| 10 bps | +1.79% | +1.59% | 0.59 |
| 25 bps | +1.79% | +1.29% | 0.48 |

A round-trip cost of even 25 bps each way shaves ~0.5pp off a multi-month hold — costs are
**not** the binding constraint. The binding constraints are the **break tail** (a single
blocked deal can erase a year of spread income) and **capacity / diversification**: a real
merger-arb book needs *many* simultaneous deals to diversify the idiosyncratic break risk,
and the edge per deal is thin enough that it is easily lost to a clustered wave of breaks
(antitrust regimes, financing freezes) that hit the whole book at once.

## Synthetic positive control — fair bet vs planted edge

A deterministic deal book (n = 250, break probability 8%, break loss −28%) with the spread
**pinned to fair-insurance value** so that `edge = 0` is a genuinely fair bet:

| planted edge / deal | mean | Welch *t* | bootstrap *p*(≤0) | breaks |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (fair bet) | +0.52% | **1.10** | 0.142 | 14 |
| **+0.02** | +2.41% | **4.77** | 0.000 | 14 |
| **+0.05** | +5.24% | **9.56** | 0.000 | 14 |

With **no** planted edge the test stays **below t = 2** (it does not manufacture
significance from a spread that merely pays for its tail), and a planted **+2%/deal** edge
lights it up at *t* = 4.8. The control proves the engine is unbiased **and** that the
real-tape *t* of 0.67 is exactly what an *absent-or-tiny* per-deal edge looks like through a
20-deal keyhole.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The mean realized arb return is **positive (+1.79%)** and the win-rate
  is high (**80%**) — the folklore is partly real — but the per-deal mean **fails t ≥ 2**
  (*t* = 0.67, bootstrap *p* = 0.24, 90% CI [−2.6%, +5.9%]), the distribution is left-skewed,
  and the headline spread is gross of a break tail that erases most of it. The book is small
  and survivorship-shaped (acquired targets delist; we use documented closes). Literature
  support + a positive-but-insignificant point estimate ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are negligible, but the edge per deal is thin and the
  return is **short a deal-break put**: a single blocked deal (−20% to −40%) erases a year of
  spread, and breaks cluster (antitrust waves, financing freezes) so the tail is not
  diversified by simply holding more deals. A spread coupon whose mean is inside its own
  noise and whose risk is a fat left tail is **not a NAV-scale free lunch**.
- **"Free lunch"? — BUSTED.** The "steady market-neutral spread" is **insurance premium in a
  costume**: you are paid the spread for **writing a deal-break put**, and on an honest tape
  the premium roughly equals the expected loss. The 80% win-rate with rare deep losers is the
  classic short-volatility / picking-up-pennies payoff — real as a strategy *style*, not a
  free lunch.
